The Solidarity Press Agency's dispatches to Radio Free Europe, an American-funded broadcaster aimed at Eastern Europe, stopped after that first night.{c:168}{c:169}{c:170}
stated_justification: Jaruzelski told the country in his televised address that Poland had reached the edge of an abyss and that the structures of the state were ceasing to function, presenting martial law as necessary to prevent collapse.{c:168}
effect_on_reporting: Nearly every Polish newspaper stopped publishing, phone and telex communication was cut nationwide, thousands of people including most Solidarity-linked journalists were interned, and foreign correspondents were reduced within a week to filing restricted reports based only on state media.{c:169}

title: United Kingdom bars broadcasters from airing Sinn Féin members' own voices
issue_of_the_day: Violence linked to the conflict in Northern Ireland, often called the Troubles, continued through the 1980s, and the British government wanted to deny paramilitary-linked political figures what it considered a broadcasting platform.
outcome_note: The broadcasting ban was lifted on September 16, 1994, shortly after the Irish Republican Army's August 1994 ceasefire declaration.
summary: Home Secretary Douglas Hurd directed British broadcasters in October 1988 not to air the voices of representatives of Sinn Féin, a party linked to the Irish Republican Army, and other groups linked to violence in Northern Ireland. Broadcasters got around it by having actors read transcripts of the same interviews.{c:171}{c:172}{c:173}
what_happened: As violence continued in Northern Ireland during Margaret Thatcher's government, Home Secretary Douglas Hurd issued a directive in October 1988 barring the British Broadcasting Corporation and independent broadcasters from airing the voices of representatives of Sinn Féin, a political party linked to the Irish Republican Army, along with several other organizations linked to paramilitary violence on both sides of the conflict. The order stopped short of banning coverage of what those representatives said, so broadcasters had actors read transcripts of interviews using the same words spoken on camera by the banned speakers, including actor Stephen Rea voicing Sinn Féin leader Gerry Adams. Some viewers found the practice unintentionally sympathetic, since a calm actor's reading could soften how a speaker's own voice might have sounded. The restriction, which also covered some pro-British loyalist groups, remained in place for six years and was lifted in September 1994 shortly after the Irish Republican Army declared a ceasefire.{c:171}{c:172}{c:173}
stated_justification: Hurd's Home Office said organizations that supported violence through the bomb and the gun could not in all circumstances be given the same broadcasting rights as everyone else.{c:171}
effect_on_reporting: British broadcasters could not air the actual voices of Sinn Féin representatives and some loyalist paramilitary-linked figures for six years, instead using actors to read the same words from interview transcripts.{c:172}

title: South Africa's Suppression of Communism Act lets the government ban publications and restrict individuals
issue_of_the_day: South Africa's National Party government, elected in 1948 on a platform of apartheid racial segregation, used the act to suppress the Communist Party of South Africa and, more broadly, organized political opposition to its policies.
outcome_note: The "Internal Security and Intimidation Amendment Act" repealed section 55 of the Suppression of Communism Act, which had prohibited furthering the aims of communism, on July 31, 1991; broader banning orders under the act and its successors had already been lifted the year before, in February 1990.{c:731}
summary: Under Prime Minister Daniel François Malan, South Africa's parliament approved the Suppression of Communism Act in 1950, defining communism broadly enough to cover most opposition to apartheid. It let the government ban organizations and publications and forbid banned individuals from being quoted at all.{c:174}{c:175}{c:176}
what_happened: South Africa's parliament, under the National Party government of Prime Minister Daniel François Malan, approved the Suppression of Communism Act, which commenced on July 17, 1950, two years after the party came to power on its apartheid platform. The law defined communism so broadly that it covered almost any opposition to the government's racial policies, not only formal Communist Party activity. It empowered the government to detain and to ban individuals and organizations it judged likely to further communism as the act defined it, and made it a criminal offense to publish, print or in any way distribute anything said or written by a banned person, effectively erasing them from public print entirely. The Communist Party of South Africa itself dissolved days after the law's approval rather than operate under it. Over the following four decades, more than 2,000 people were subjected to banning orders under the act and its successors before the last such bans were lifted in February 1990.{c:174}{c:175}{c:176}{c:730}
stated_justification: The government said the act was needed to suppress communism, which the law itself defined broadly enough to include any activity aimed at bringing about political, industrial, social or economic change through means the Act deemed banned, or disorder, covering most organized opposition to apartheid.{c:175}
effect_on_reporting: Newspapers and other publications could not legally publish anything said or written by a person the government had banned, suppressing banned anti-apartheid activists and writers in the South African press entirely for as long as their bans lasted.{c:176}

title: Egypt's Nasser government nationalizes every newspaper and magazine in the country
issue_of_the_day: Nasser's government was consolidating state control over Egypt's economy and institutions in the years following the 1952 revolution, and extended that control to the press as an instrument of its nationalist program.
outcome_note: State ownership structures created by the 1960 decree, including the government-appointed leadership of major papers such as Al-Ahram, remained in place through the 1980s.
summary: President Gamal Abdel Nasser's government issued a decree on May 24, 1960 placing every newspaper and magazine in Egypt under state ownership and management, with the government appointing editors and deciding content, ending private control of the country's press.{c:177}{c:178}{c:179}
what_happened: Egypt's president, Gamal Abdel Nasser, had led the Free Officers movement that overthrew King Farouk in 1952 and increasingly used the media to advance his nationalist program. On May 24, 1960, his government issued a presidential decree nationalizing all newspapers and magazines in the country, placing them under the full management of the state, which chose their editors and set their content. Al-Ahram, Egypt's most prominent daily, became the de facto voice of the government under the nationalized system, with Nasser having already appointed the influential journalist Muhammad Hassanein Heikal as its editor in 1957. The decree ended private ownership of the Egyptian press outright, a structure of state control over the country's major papers that persisted for decades afterward, even as later governments allowed some opposition and independent titles to operate alongside the nationalized press.{c:177}{c:178}{c:179}
stated_justification: Nasser's government presented the nationalization as part of a broader program of state control over the economy and public life following the 1952 revolution, using the press as an instrument to advance its nationalist agenda.{c:179}
effect_on_reporting: Every Egyptian newspaper and magazine came under direct state management, with the government choosing editors and defining acceptable content, ending independent ownership of the country's press.{c:178}

title: South Africa bans television and photographic coverage of unrest under a state of emergency
issue_of_the_day: Unrest against apartheid had spread through South Africa's Black townships through 1985, and the government's emergency regulations applied to the television and photographic coverage that had brought international attention to the violence.
outcome_note: South Africa's state of emergency and its media restrictions ended in June 1990 as State President F. W. de Klerk began dismantling apartheid.
summary: Under a state of emergency State President P. W. Botha had declared in July 1985, the government banned television, radio and photographic coverage of unrest in South Africa's Black townships on November 2, 1985, requiring print journalists to report only under police escort.{c:180}{c:181}{c:182}
what_happened: State President P. W. Botha's government declared a state of emergency in parts of South Africa on July 21, 1985, in response to widening unrest against apartheid in Black townships. On November 2, 1985, Minister of Law and Order Louis le Grange announced new emergency regulations banning television, radio and photographic coverage of riot situations entirely, saying camera crews had become a catalyst for further violence. A government notice made it an offense to record any riot situation by sound or image, with penalties of up to a $7,000 fine or 10 years in prison. Print journalists were still permitted to report on unrest, but only under police escort. International news organizations, including UPI and NBC News, protested that the restrictions made objective reporting far harder, while South Africa's Foreign Correspondents Association warned the measure marked the start of what it called a slide toward a completely controlled press.{c:180}{c:181}{c:182}
stated_justification: Le Grange said the government was concerned that the presence of television and other camera crews in unrest situations had become a catalyst for further violence, and framed the ban as a way to reduce that effect.{c:180}
effect_on_reporting: Television, radio and photographic coverage of unrest in South African townships was banned outright, with violators facing large fines or years in prison, while print reporters could cover unrest only under police escort.{c:182}

title: India imposes pre-press controls on every newspaper during the 1975 Emergency
issue_of_the_day: A court had found Prime Minister Gandhi guilty of election malpractice shortly before the Emergency began, and her government cited threats to internal stability in declaring the state of emergency and imposing press controls the next day.
outcome_note: Gandhi ended the Emergency and lifted press controls on March 21, 1977, shortly before her party lost the general election that followed.
summary: Prime Minister Indira Gandhi declared a state of emergency on June 25, 1975, and the next day her government imposed pre-press controls on every Indian newspaper, requiring official clearance before publication and later forcibly merging the country's news agencies into one.{c:183}
what_happened: Prime Minister Indira Gandhi's government declared a national state of emergency on June 25, 1975, citing threats to internal stability after a court had found her guilty of election malpractice. On June 26, 1975, the government imposed pre-press controls on every newspaper in the country, requiring editors to obtain government clearance before publishing news reports, editorials or photographs. Government-appointed national and regional censors reviewed content and classified newspapers as friendly, neutral or critical depending on their editorial stance toward the government. Foreign correspondents faced prior screening of their telex dispatches from July 5, 1975, and the government cut power to newspaper offices in Delhi during the early days of enforcement. The Press Council of India, a statutory body meant to safeguard press standards, was abolished during the period, and on February 1, 1976, the government merged the country's four major news agencies into a single state-controlled entity called Samachar.{c:183}{c:184}{c:185}
stated_justification: Gandhi's government said the emergency measures, including press controls, were necessary to protect internal stability and public order at a time it described as a serious threat to the country.{c:183}{c:184}{c:185}
effect_on_reporting: Every Indian newspaper had to submit content for government clearance before publication, foreign correspondents' dispatches faced prior screening, the Press Council of India was abolished, and the country's news agencies were merged into a single state-controlled body.{c:184}

title: Philippines President Marcos closes every major news outlet under martial law
issue_of_the_day: Marcos had declared martial law citing threats from Communist insurgency and civil unrest, and moved immediately to eliminate independent media coverage that might question the declaration or his expanding powers.
outcome_note: Marcos was removed from power in the People Power Revolution of February 22-25, 1986, ending martial-law controls on the Philippine press.
summary: President Ferdinand Marcos declared martial law on September 21, 1972, and the next day ordered the military to take over nearly every newspaper, radio and television station in the Philippines, jailing prominent publishers and editors and requiring government clearance for whatever remained.{c:186}{c:187}{c:188}
what_happened: President Ferdinand Marcos signed Proclamation No. 1081, placing the Philippines under martial law, on September 21, 1972. The following day, Letter of Instruction No. 1 ordered the military to take over privately owned newspapers, magazines, and radio and television stations nationwide, on the stated ground of preventing their use for state messaging against the government. Major newspapers including the Manila Times, the Manila Chronicle and the Manila Daily Bulletin were closed, along with the country's wire agencies. Publishers and editors known for criticism of Marcos, including Teodoro Locsin Sr. of the Philippines Free Press and Manila Times publisher Chino Roces, were detained in military camps. On September 25, the Department of Public Information ordered that whatever media remained had to obtain clearance before publishing and could carry no editorial commentary critical of the military or law enforcement, controls that continued through the 14-year martial-law period.{c:186}{c:187}{c:188}
stated_justification: Marcos's Letter of Instruction No. 1 said the media takeover was needed to prevent privately owned newspapers, magazines and broadcast stations from being used for state messaging purposes against the government.{c:186}
effect_on_reporting: Nearly every major newspaper, radio and television station in the country was shut down or placed under military control, prominent editors and publishers were detained, and surviving outlets needed government clearance before publishing anything.{c:187}

title: South Korea's martial-law government purges journalists who resisted press controls
issue_of_the_day: Chun Doo-hwan's military government had just suppressed a pro-democracy uprising centered in the city of Kwangju in May 1980, and used the purge to remove journalists it associated with resistance to press controls during that period.
outcome_note: South Korea's June 1987 democracy movement led to direct presidential elections and an easing of press controls; a 1986 leak of secret press guidelines had already embarrassed the government.
summary: Under General Chun Doo-hwan's martial-law government, South Korean authorities ordered newsrooms in 1980 to purge journalists who had resisted press controls or joined a May sit-in strike for press freedom, and closed 172 periodicals, dismissing roughly 2,000 journalists in total.{c:189}{c:190}{c:191}
what_happened: General Chun Doo-hwan's martial-law government, which had seized effective control of South Korea after President Park Chung-hee's October 1979 assassination and a May 1980 military response to pro-democracy protests centered in Kwangju, ordered South Korean news organizations in the summer of 1980 to purge journalists who had resisted press controls or sought press freedom. Newsrooms were told to dismiss staff by August 10, 1980, including those who had taken part in a sit-in strike from May 19 to 28 demanding freedom of the press, with the government's ruling committee drawing up purge lists where newsrooms' own dismissals fell short of the military's standards. The Culture and Information Ministry also ordered the closure of 172 periodicals. An association formed by the dismissed journalists later counted about 2,000 people who lost their careers in the press during the purge, some of whom were also sent to reeducation camps.{c:189}{c:190}{c:191}
stated_justification: The government said nothing was more important than maintaining national security against North Korea and preserving domestic order and peace, the standard it used to justify purging journalists who had sought press freedom.{c:190}
effect_on_reporting: An association of the journalists dismissed in the purge later counted about 2,000 who could no longer work in the South Korean press, while 172 periodicals were closed by government order.{c:191}

title: Burma's new military government tightens pre-publication press controls after seizing power
issue_of_the_day: SLORC had just taken power after crushing the August 1988 pro-democracy uprising, sometimes called 8888 for its start date, and used the Press Scrutiny Board to prevent coverage sympathetic to the uprising or critical of military rule.
outcome_note: The Press Scrutiny Board's pre-publication press controls remained fully in force at the end of 1989 and continued operating for decades afterward.
summary: After crushing the 1988 pro-democracy uprising, Burma's new military government, the State Law and Order Restoration Council, tightened an existing pre-publication press controls board and raised penalties for unauthorized publishing to seven years in prison, while denying any press controls existed.{c:192}{c:193}{c:194}
what_happened: General Saw Maung's State Law and Order Restoration Council, known as SLORC, seized power in Burma on September 18, 1988, after the military crushed a nationwide pro-democracy uprising that had begun that August. The new government relied on the Press Scrutiny Board, a press controls body operating since 1962, which required every book, magazine, periodical, song and film to be submitted for approval before release and could reject, cancel or delay permission to publish without giving a reason. In June 1989, the government raised penalties under the Printers and Publishers Registration Law to as much as seven years in prison, or fines of 30,000 kyats, for each violation. Publishers whose material the board found objectionable had entire pages torn out or covered in silver ink to obscure banned names or content. At least a dozen writers, publishers and distributors were imprisoned under the law by the mid-1990s, even as the government publicly denied that it restricted the press at all.{c:192}{c:193}{c:194}
stated_justification: SLORC publicly denied that any government controls of the press, radio or television existed in Burma, even as its Press Scrutiny Board reviewed and could reject all published material before release.{c:194}
effect_on_reporting: Every book, magazine, periodical, song and film had to be submitted to the Press Scrutiny Board before release, publications faced pages torn out or covered in silver ink for objectionable content, and writers faced years in prison for unauthorized publishing.{c:192}

title: China expels foreign journalists and restricts coverage of the Tiananmen Square protests
issue_of_the_day: Student-led pro-democracy protests had occupied Tiananmen Square for weeks before the government declared martial law and then used the military to clear the square in early June 1989, and moved to control international coverage of the events that followed.
outcome_note: Martial law in Beijing was lifted in January 1990, but broad Chinese government controls on foreign press coverage continued well beyond that date.
summary: After declaring martial law in Beijing on May 20, 1989, China's government imposed rigid restrictions on coverage of pro-democracy protests and, following the military's June 3-4 clearing of Tiananmen Square, expelled Associated Press correspondent John Pomfret and Voice of America correspondent Alan Pessin.{c:195}{c:196}{c:197}
what_happened: China's government, headed by Premier Li Peng, declared martial law in Beijing on May 20, 1989, as student-led pro-democracy protests centered on Tiananmen Square continued, and imposed rigid restrictions on how foreign and domestic media could cover the demonstrations. After the military cleared the square by force on June 3 and 4, 1989, an operation that led to over 900 arrests within days, the government ordered two American journalists, Associated Press correspondent John Pomfret and Voice of America correspondent Alan Pessin, to leave the country within 72 hours on June 14, 1989. Authorities accused Pomfret of frequent contacts with the leaders of organizations it had banned and of obtaining state secrets through means it prohibited, and accused Pessin of writing stories the government said distorted facts and incited unrest. The official Communist Party newspaper, People's Daily, separately protested the United States embassy's decision to shelter dissident scientist Fang Lizhi as a violation of Chinese sovereignty.{c:195}{c:196}{c:197}
stated_justification: Chinese authorities accused Pomfret of obtaining state secrets through means it prohibited and maintaining contact with organizers from groups it had banned, and accused Pessin of distorting facts and inciting unrest through his reporting.{c:196}
effect_on_reporting: Two American correspondents were given 72 hours to leave China, foreign and domestic media operated under rigid martial-law restrictions on covering the protests and the military operation that ended them, and broader controls on reporting the events continued in their aftermath.{c:197}

title: Israel retains a British-era law giving the military the power to review and restrict the press
issue_of_the_day: Israel's 1948 declaration of independence and the war that followed created an immediate perceived security need, which the retained British-era Press Ordinance and later Editors' Committee arrangement were meant to address by keeping military information out of print.
outcome_note: The military press-review system built on the 1948 Press Ordinance and the 1953 Editors' Committee remained in force through the 1980s and beyond.
summary: When Israel declared independence in 1948 under Prime Minister David Ben-Gurion, it retained a British Mandate-era Press Ordinance giving the military the power to review and restrict publications on security grounds, later formalized through an Editors' Committee that let most Israeli newspapers self-restrict security matters.{c:198}
what_happened: When Israel declared independence in 1948, its new government under Prime Minister David Ben-Gurion retained the Press Ordinance, a law from the British Mandate period that gave a military press reviewer the power to review and block publication of material on security grounds. In 1953, the military and the Israeli press formalized their relationship by creating the Editors' Committee, an agreement under which mainstream Israeli newspapers could largely review their own security content, submitting to the military press reviewer only articles that touched directly on national security matters. Newspapers and other outlets operating in the West Bank and Gaza Strip, which came under Israeli military administration after the 1967 war, received no comparable self-press controls privilege; their editors had to submit every article to military press reviewers each night before publication. The system, with dozens of categories of information still legally requiring submission to the military press reviewer, remained a distinctive feature of Israeli press regulation for decades.{c:198}{c:199}{c:200}
stated_justification: The Press Ordinance and its later Editors' Committee arrangement were justified on national security grounds, aimed at preventing publication of information the military judged could aid Israel's adversaries.{c:198}{c:199}{c:200}
effect_on_reporting: Mainstream Israeli newspapers could largely handle everyday coverage on their own but had to submit security-related articles to the military press reviewer, while Palestinian publications in the occupied territories had to submit every article for review each night.{c:200}

title: Australia's wartime government seizes a Sydney newspaper edition under press controls rules
issue_of_the_day: Australia remained at war in the Pacific in 1944, and its wartime press controls apparatus, already the subject of tension with newspaper proprietors, moved against the Sunday Telegraph for material it judged to breach the press controls rules.
outcome_note: The High Court of Australia granted an injunction days after the seizure, blocking further suppression of the newspaper's editions.
summary: Australia's wartime government, under Prime Minister John Curtin, controlled press coverage of military events through the Department of Information. In April 1944, Minister for Information Arthur Calwell ordered the seizure of copies of the Sydney Sunday Telegraph for breaching press controls rules, prompting newspapers' joint protest and a High Court injunction against the seizure.{c:201}{c:202}{c:203}
what_happened: Australia's wartime government, led by Prime Minister John Curtin, ran press and radio press controls through the Department of Information under National Security Regulations, monitoring war correspondents and controlling what could be published about military events. Arthur Calwell, the minister responsible for information, brought what colleagues described as an ingrained distrust of the press to the role. On April 16, 1944, Calwell ordered the seizure of copies of the Sydney Sunday Telegraph for breaching the wartime press controls rules. Sydney's newspapers responded the next morning with a joint statement challenging the censors' authority to act that way, and the High Court of Australia, the country's highest court, granted an injunction preventing further suppression of the paper's editions. The same wartime press controls system had already brought the government into repeated conflict with newspaper proprietors, including over an unsuccessful attempt to merge Melbourne's three morning newspapers, the Age, the Argus and the Sun, for the duration of the war.{c:201}{c:202}{c:203}
stated_justification: Calwell's Department of Information said the seized edition of the Sunday Telegraph had breached the wartime press controls regulations governing what newspapers could publish about military and security matters.{c:203}
effect_on_reporting: Copies of the Sunday Telegraph were seized before the High Court's injunction stopped further suppression, and the episode became part of a wider pattern of confrontation between the wartime press controls system and Australian newspaper proprietors.{c:202}

title: United States military restricts reporters to escorted press pools during the Gulf War
issue_of_the_day: U.S.-led coalition forces' campaign to expel Iraqi forces from Kuwait after Iraq's August 1990 invasion.
outcome_note: The pool system stayed in place through the war's end on February 28, 1991; the legal challenge in Nation Magazine v. Department of Defense was later dismissed as moot.
summary: The U.S. military required reporters covering the 1991 Gulf War to work in escorted "pools" rather than move freely, reviewed pool dispatches before release, and reporters who left the pools were captured or detained.{c:204}{c:205}{c:206}{c:207}
what_happened: During the Gulf War (January to February 1991), the Pentagon, the U.S. Department of Defense, required most journalists covering U.S. forces to join escorted press pools rather than travel independently. Public affairs officers accompanied every pooled reporter, and dispatches passed through a security review before release, officials said, "for its conformance to ... ground rules, not for its potential to express criticism or cause embarrassment." Assistant Secretary of Defense Pete Williams said free movement risked lives; Defense Secretary Dick Cheney said withholding operational detail served the same purpose. Journalists including CBS's Bob Simon left the pool system and were captured by Iraqi forces; others who evaded escorts were arrested by U.S. military police. The Nation and other publications sued the Department of Defense in Nation Magazine v. United States Department of Defense, arguing the pool system violated the First Amendment, the U.S. constitutional guarantee of press freedom.{c:204}{c:205}{c:206}{c:207}
stated_justification: Assistant Secretary of Defense Pete Williams said unrestricted reporters risked their own lives and troops' lives; Defense Secretary Dick Cheney said releasing operational detail could help Iraqi forces: "every detail we offer would increase the likelihood that the military forces of Iraq could learn more about our operations."{c:205}
effect_on_reporting: Reporters could reach the front only through pools with military escorts and pre-release review of dispatches; those who worked outside the system, including a CBS crew, were captured or detained, and coverage relied heavily on Pentagon briefings.{c:204}{c:207}

title: Pentagon sets ground rules for journalists embedded with United States forces in Iraq
issue_of_the_day: The buildup to and launch of the U.S.-led invasion of Iraq in March 2003.
outcome_note: The embedding program ran through the invasion and became the Pentagon's standard model for media access in later conflicts.
summary: Ahead of the 2003 invasion of Iraq, the Pentagon assigned about 600 journalists to travel with United States military units under written ground rules restricting what they could report about troop numbers, operations and casualties.{c:208}{c:209}{c:210}{c:211}
what_happened: In February 2003, before the U.S.-led invasion of Iraq, the Pentagon, the U.S. Department of Defense, issued written ground rules for reporters embedded with military units. The rules barred disclosing specific troop numbers below corps level, future operations, rules of engagement and identifying details of casualties or captured enemy prisoners for 72 hours or until families were notified. The Pentagon said the limits were meant "for the safety and security of U.S. forces and embedded media" and were "in no way intended to prevent release of derogatory, embarrassing, negative or uncomplimentary information." About 600 journalists joined the program, travelling with units through the invasion that began March 20, 2003. Embargoes on operational details were to lift once the security concern passed. Critics said access depended on units' cooperation and that embedded reporters saw only a narrow slice of the war; supporters said embedding produced far more front-line coverage than the restricted pools of the 1991 Gulf War.{c:208}{c:209}{c:210}{c:211}
stated_justification: The Pentagon said the ground rules existed "for the safety and security of U.S. forces and embedded media" and were "in no way intended to prevent release of derogatory, embarrassing, negative or uncomplimentary information."{c:209}
effect_on_reporting: Embedded reporters gained sustained front-line access in exchange for accepting restrictions on troop numbers, future operations and casualty details, and for accepting embargoes lifted only once the military judged the security concern had passed.{c:208}{c:210}{c:211}

title: New York Times reporter Judith Miller jailed for refusing to name a confidential source in the Valerie Plame affair
issue_of_the_day: The Bush administration's case for the 2003 Iraq War and the public dispute over former ambassador Joseph Wilson's contrary account of Iraqi uranium claims.
outcome_note: Courts upheld the contempt order and subpoena; Miller served 85 days before her source freed her to testify, and prosecutors later convicted Libby of perjury.
summary: A federal judge jailed New York Times reporter Judith Miller for contempt after she refused to tell a grand jury who told her the identity of CIA officer Valerie Plame, part of a special counsel's investigation into the leak.{c:212}{c:213}{c:214}{c:215}
what_happened: In 2003, columnist Robert Novak published the name of Valerie Plame, an undercover Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) officer, after officials in President George W. Bush's administration discussed her identity with reporters after her husband publicly criticized the Iraq War. Special counsel Patrick Fitzgerald investigated the leak and subpoenaed several reporters, including Judith Miller of The New York Times, to testify before a federal grand jury, a panel that decides whether to bring criminal charges. Miller had not published a story about Plame but had discussed her with a source, Vice President Dick Cheney's chief of staff I. Lewis "Scooter" Libby, and refused to identify him, citing a reporter's duty to protect sources. On July 6, 2005, federal judge Thomas F. Hogan found her in civil contempt and jailed her. She was released on September 29, 2005, after Libby released her from confidentiality and she agreed to testify. Libby was later convicted of perjury and obstruction.{c:212}{c:213}{c:214}{c:215}
stated_justification: Judge Hogan held that Miller's refusal to identify her source obstructed a federal grand jury investigation into a possible crime; Miller said, "If journalists cannot be trusted to keep confidences, then journalists cannot function and there cannot be a free press."{c:212}
effect_on_reporting: Miller spent 85 days in jail for declining to reveal a source for a story she never wrote, a rare instance of a United States reporter jailed over source confidentiality, and other reporters subpoenaed in the same case negotiated releases from their sources instead.{c:213}{c:214}

title: United States charges Army analyst Chelsea Manning under the Espionage Act for leaking to WikiLeaks
issue_of_the_day: United States conduct of the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan and detainee treatment, including the CIA's interrogation program.
outcome_note: Manning's convictions were not overturned, but President Obama commuted her 35-year sentence in January 2017 and she was released that May.
summary: The U.S. Army charged intelligence analyst Chelsea Manning under the Espionage Act, a 1917 law against disclosing defense information, after she gave WikiLeaks, a website that publishes leaked documents, a large archive of military and diplomatic files that news organizations later published.{c:216}{c:217}{c:218}{c:219}
what_happened: In 2010, U.S. Army intelligence analyst Chelsea Manning gave WikiLeaks, a website that publishes leaked documents, a large archive of military reports and diplomatic cables, including video of a 2007 helicopter strike in Baghdad. The material included, the American Civil Liberties Union said, "evidence of civilian deaths in Iraq and Afghanistan, U.S. attempts to cover up the CIA torture program, and other matters of public interest." WikiLeaks and news partners including The Guardian and The New York Times published selections. The Army charged Manning under the Espionage Act, a 1917 law against disclosing defense information, and, more unusually, with "aiding the enemy," a capital military offense; prosecutors did not allege she gave material directly to any adversary. A military court convicted her in 2013 on Espionage Act counts but acquitted her of aiding the enemy, and sentenced her to 35 years, the longest sentence given a leaker in United States history. President Obama commuted the sentence in January 2017.{c:216}{c:217}{c:218}{c:219}
stated_justification: Military prosecutors said Manning's disclosures endangered lives and national security; the ACLU said the "aiding the enemy" charge was "akin to treason and punishable by death" despite no allegation she gave material to an adversary directly.{c:217}
effect_on_reporting: The prosecution set a United States record for a leak sentence and became a reference point for later Espionage Act cases against sources for journalists; the ACLU said, "When a soldier who shared information with the press and public is punished far more harshly than others who tortured prisoners and killed civilians, something is seriously wrong with our justice system."{c:218}

title: United States prosecutes former CIA officer John Kiriakou under the Espionage Act for identifying a covert colleague to a journalist
issue_of_the_day: Public disclosure of the CIA's post-September 11 interrogation program, including its use of waterboarding.
outcome_note: Kiriakou served his full 30-month sentence under the plea agreement and was released in February 2015; no CIA interrogation-program official faced comparable charges.
summary: Former CIA officer John Kiriakou, who in 2007 was the first CIA officer to publicly describe the agency's waterboarding of a detainee, pleaded guilty to identifying a covert colleague to a journalist and was sentenced under the Espionage Act to 30 months in prison.{c:220}{c:221}{c:222}{c:223}
what_happened: John Kiriakou, a former Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) officer, said publicly in a 2007 television interview that the CIA had waterboarded a detainee, the first time an agency officer had confirmed the practice, which international bodies have called torture. Federal prosecutors later charged Kiriakou under the Espionage Act, a 1917 law against disclosing defense information, for identifying a covert CIA officer to a freelance journalist investigating the interrogation program; the journalist did not publish the name. Kiriakou pleaded guilty in October 2012 to one count of passing information to a person not authorized to receive it. U.S. Attorney Neil MacBride said Kiriakou "put the life of a covert officer at risk." On January 25, 2013, Judge Leonie Brinkema sentenced him to 30 months, the statutory minimum under his plea agreement, saying she "wished she could have imposed a greater sentence." No CIA official involved in the interrogation program was prosecuted.{c:220}{c:221}{c:222}{c:223}
stated_justification: U.S. Attorney Neil MacBride said, "John Kiriakou put the life of a covert officer at risk; he put the officer's family in danger; and he exposed our nation's vital secrets." Prosecutors also said Kiriakou was motivated by "fame and money."{c:220}
effect_on_reporting: Kiriakou, not the journalist he spoke with, was prosecuted and imprisoned; press-freedom advocates said the case showed sources faced Espionage Act prosecution for contact with reporters even when no story identifying the covert officer was published.{c:221}

title: United States Justice Department secretly seizes two months of Associated Press phone records
issue_of_the_day: A May 2012 AP report on a foiled al-Qaeda bomb plot aimed at a U.S.-bound airplane, which the government said compromised an intelligence source.
outcome_note: The records were not returned and no journalist or source was charged; the Justice Department issued revised media-subpoena guidelines on July 12, 2013, after the disclosure.
summary: The U.S. Justice Department secretly obtained two months of telephone records from more than 20 Associated Press phone lines during a leak investigation, notifying the news agency only after the fact; AP called the scope of the seizure unjustified.{c:224}{c:225}{c:226}{c:227}
what_happened: In April and May 2012, the Associated Press (AP) reported that the CIA had disrupted a plot by an al-Qaeda affiliate in Yemen to bomb a U.S.-bound airplane. The Justice Department, investigating who disclosed the classified operation, obtained telephone toll records covering more than 20 AP office and staff phone lines in New York, Washington and Hartford, Connecticut, and the AP's line in the U.S. House of Representatives press gallery, without first asking AP for the records, as its own guidelines generally required. AP learned of the seizure when the Justice Department notified it on May 10, 2013, and disclosed it publicly on May 13. AP President Gary Pruitt said, "There can be no possible justification for such an over-broad collection of the telephone communications of The Associated Press and its reporters." More than 100 journalists worked in the offices whose numbers were collected. No journalist or source was ever charged in the underlying leak case.{c:224}{c:225}{c:226}{c:227}
stated_justification: Attorney General Eric Holder called the underlying disclosure "among, if not the most serious ... a ... very, very serious leak," and the Justice Department said, "We take seriously our obligations to follow all applicable laws, federal regulations, and Department of Justice policies when issuing subpoenas for phone records of media organisations."{c:224}{c:225}
effect_on_reporting: The seizure covered work and personal numbers for AP staff across three bureaus and swept in more than 100 journalists' shared office lines, exposing AP's contacts and sourcing patterns on a wide range of unrelated stories, not only the leak under investigation.{c:226}{c:227}

title: United States search warrant names Fox News reporter James Rosen a possible co-conspirator in a leak case
issue_of_the_day: A 2009 Fox News report, sourced to a State Department analyst, forecasting North Korea's response to new United Nations sanctions.
outcome_note: The warrant was not withdrawn from the record; Kim pleaded guilty in 2014 and Rosen was never charged. Holder's July 2013 guidelines later restricted subpoenas naming reporters as suspects.
summary: A 2010 FBI search-warrant affidavit, unsealed in 2013, described Fox News reporter James Rosen as a possible co-conspirator in violating the Espionage Act because he sought classified information from a State Department analyst, and used that theory to obtain his private emails.{c:228}{c:229}{c:230}
what_happened: In 2009, Fox News reporter James Rosen published a story, based on a State Department analyst's account, that North Korea would likely respond to United Nations sanctions with more nuclear tests. Investigating the leak, an FBI agent wrote in a 2010 warrant affidavit, unsealed and reported in 2013, that Rosen, "in his newsgathering, was violating federal statutes that prohibit 'unauthorized disclosure of national defense information' as an 'aider, abettor, and/or co-conspirator,'" under the Espionage Act, a 1917 law against disclosing defense information. A federal magistrate approved the warrant, which the Justice Department used to obtain two days of Rosen's personal emails, his phone records and records of his security-badge movements inside the State Department. The analyst, Stephen Kim, was separately charged and later pleaded guilty. Rosen himself was never charged; press-freedom groups said naming a reporter as a criminal co-conspirator for ordinary newsgathering, asking questions and cultivating a source, had no precedent in a warrant against a working journalist.{c:228}{c:229}{c:230}
stated_justification: The FBI affidavit argued Rosen's newsgathering itself, soliciting classified information and cultivating a source, made him a likely "aider, abettor, and/or co-conspirator" in violating the Espionage Act, the legal theory the Justice Department used to justify seizing his records.{c:229}
effect_on_reporting: The Justice Department seized Rosen's personal emails, phone records and State Department security-badge logs; the Committee to Protect Journalists said such tactics against reporters had "a chilling effect domestically and sends a terrible message to journalists around the world."{c:230}

title: United States pursues New York Times reporter James Risen's testimony for years before dropping its demand for his source
issue_of_the_day: A 2006 book account of a botched CIA operation meant to disrupt Iran's nuclear weapons program.
outcome_note: After the Supreme Court declined to hear Risen's appeal, the Justice Department chose not to compel his testimony or the identity of his source; Sterling was convicted without it.
summary: For years, federal prosecutors sought New York Times reporter James Risen's testimony identifying a confidential source in a CIA leak case; the Supreme Court declined to hear his appeal, but Attorney General Eric Holder ultimately chose not to force him to testify or name the source.{c:231}{c:232}{c:233}{c:234}
what_happened: James Risen, a reporter for The New York Times, wrote in a 2006 book and in earlier newspaper articles about a botched CIA operation aimed at Iran's nuclear program, citing an unnamed source. Federal prosecutors identified former CIA officer Jeffrey Sterling as a suspect and, starting in 2008, subpoenaed Risen to testify before a grand jury and later at Sterling's trial, seeking to make him confirm Sterling was his source. Risen refused and fought the subpoena through the courts; the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit ruled in 2013 that reporters had no First Amendment privilege to withhold a source's identity in a criminal case, and the Supreme Court declined to hear his appeal in 2014. Attorney General Eric Holder then approved only a limited subpoena that did not ask Risen to identify his source, and in October 2014 said prosecutors would not force him to testify at all. Sterling was convicted in January 2015 using other evidence, without Risen's testimony.{c:231}{c:232}{c:233}{c:234}
stated_justification: Prosecutors said Risen's direct testimony was necessary to prove Sterling was his source; Attorney General Eric Holder said of the resolution, "the way in which that case was handled after the new policies were put in place [is] an example of how the Justice Department can proceed."{c:231}
effect_on_reporting: Risen faced years of legal jeopardy, including the threat of jail for contempt, before prosecutors relented; the case became a benchmark for how far the government would press reporters to identify sources in national-security leak prosecutions.{c:232}

title: White House revokes CNN correspondent Jim Acosta's press credential after a news conference exchange with President Trump
issue_of_the_day: President Trump's characterization of a migrant caravan approaching the United States border in the days before the November 2018 midterm election.
outcome_note: A federal judge issued a temporary restraining order on November 16, 2018, and the White House permanently restored Acosta's credential three days later rather than continue the lawsuit.
summary: After CNN's Jim Acosta questioned President Trump at a news conference and briefly kept hold of a microphone as an intern reached for it, the White House suspended his hard pass, the standing credential letting reporters enter the grounds; a federal judge ordered it restored a week later.{c:235}{c:236}{c:237}
what_happened: At a November 7, 2018 White House news conference, President Trump and CNN correspondent Jim Acosta argued over Acosta's questions about immigration; when a White House intern reached to take his microphone, Acosta held onto it and briefly touched her arm. That evening, Press Secretary Sarah Sanders announced the suspension of Acosta's hard pass, the standing credential letting reporters enter the White House grounds, saying the White House would "never tolerate a reporter placing his hands on a young woman just trying to do her job." CNN called the suspension "a threat to our democracy" and sued the White House on November 13, arguing the revocation violated the First Amendment, the constitutional guarantee of press freedom, and the Fifth Amendment's guarantee of due process. On November 16, federal judge Timothy Kelly ordered the pass restored while the case proceeded; Acosta told reporters, "Let's go back to work." The White House restored the pass permanently on November 19 rather than continue the litigation.{c:235}{c:236}{c:237}
stated_justification: Press Secretary Sarah Sanders said, "We will, however, never tolerate a reporter placing his hands on a young woman just trying to do her job as a White House intern." Government lawyers separately argued Acosta had no First Amendment right of access to the White House.{c:235}
effect_on_reporting: CNN said the revocation was "a threat to our democracy," and other outlets, including some critical of Acosta's conduct, joined an emergency court filing warning that a president could use credential revocation to penalize unfavorable questioning.{c:236}

title: United States indicts WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange under the Espionage Act
issue_of_the_day: WikiLeaks' 2010 publication of leaked United States military reports and diplomatic cables supplied by Chelsea Manning.
outcome_note: Assange spent five years in a British prison fighting extradition before a June 2024 plea deal: he pleaded guilty to one count, was sentenced to time served, and was released.
summary: The United States indicted WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange on 17 counts under the Espionage Act over the 2010 publication of leaked military and diplomatic files, charges press-freedom groups said could expose ordinary national-security journalism to prosecution.{c:238}{c:239}{c:240}{c:241}
what_happened: On May 23, 2019, the U.S. Justice Department added 17 counts under the Espionage Act, a 1917 law against disclosing defense information, to an existing charge against Julian Assange, founder of WikiLeaks, a website that publishes leaked documents. The new counts concerned WikiLeaks' 2010 publication of classified military reports and diplomatic cables supplied by U.S. Army analyst Chelsea Manning. Assistant Attorney General John Demers said, "Julian Assange is no journalist," and the department said his actions "risked serious harm to United States national security to the benefit of our adversaries." Assange's attorney, Barry Pollack, said the charges "demonstrate the gravity of the threat the criminal prosecution of Julian Assange poses to all journalists," since the conduct charged, receiving and publishing classified material from a source, is conduct news organizations routinely engage in. Assange was then in British custody after his April 2019 arrest at Ecuador's London embassy; the United States sought his extradition.{c:238}{c:239}{c:240}{c:241}
stated_justification: Assistant Attorney General John Demers said, "Julian Assange is no journalist, this is made plain by the totality of his conduct as alleged in the indictment," and the department said his actions "risked serious harm to United States national security to the benefit of our adversaries."{c:238}{c:239}
effect_on_reporting: Assange's attorney and press-freedom groups said charging the receipt and publication of leaked classified material under the Espionage Act, rather than only its unauthorized disclosure, could expose ordinary national-security journalism to prosecution.{c:240}

title: Turkey closes more than 100 media outlets by decree after a failed coup attempt
issue_of_the_day: The failed July 15, 2016 coup attempt against President Erdogan's government and the mass arrests and dismissals that followed against alleged participants and sympathizers.
outcome_note: Most closures were not reversed by the decrees themselves; Human Rights Watch documented that the closures reached opposition and Kurdish-audience outlets beyond any shown Gulen movement link.
summary: After a failed July 2016 coup attempt, Turkey's government closed more than 100 newspapers, television and radio stations, news agencies and publishing houses by state-of-emergency decree, citing alleged links to the movement it blamed for the coup.{c:242}{c:243}{c:244}{c:245}
what_happened: On July 15, 2016, a faction of Turkey's military attempted to seize power; the government put down the attempt within hours. President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's government declared a state of emergency on July 21, giving it power to rule by decree, an executive order with the force of law that bypasses ordinary parliamentary debate. Decree No. 668, issued July 27, 2016, closed 131 media outlets, including 45 newspapers, 16 television channels, three news agencies, 23 radio stations, 15 magazines and 29 publishing houses, all accused of having "links to a terrorist organization" and posing "a threat to national security." The government said the outlets had ties to the movement of the US-based cleric Fethullah Gulen, whom it accused of directing the coup attempt. Further decrees followed, including a September 28 order closing stations popular among Kurdish and Alevi audiences and opposition supporters; by December 2016, 140 outlets and 29 publishers had been shut. Human Rights Watch said the closures extended well beyond outlets with any documented Gulen movement connection.{c:242}{c:243}{c:244}{c:245}
stated_justification: The government said the closed outlets had "links to a terrorist organization" and posed "a threat to national security," tying them to the movement of U.S.-based cleric Fethullah Gulen, whom it accused of directing the coup attempt.{c:243}
effect_on_reporting: More than 100 newspapers, broadcasters, news agencies and publishing houses lost their operating licenses at a stroke, and Reporters Without Borders said the decrees eliminated "an entire swathe" of Turkey's media in one action.{c:244}

title: Nigeria's military government convicts journalists by special tribunal over coup-plot reporting
issue_of_the_day: An alleged March 1995 coup plot against General Sani Abacha's military government, which the journalists had reported on.
outcome_note: The journalists were released in stages after General Abacha's death in June 1998 under his successor's government; their convictions were not vacated in the sources reviewed.
summary: A special military tribunal convicted four Nigerian journalists as accessories to a supposed 1995 coup plot after they reported on it, sentencing them to lengthy prison terms with no right of appeal, under the military government of General Sani Abacha.{c:246}{c:247}{c:248}{c:249}
what_happened: In March 1995, Nigeria's military government, led by General Sani Abacha, announced it had uncovered a coup plot and arrested dozens of soldiers and civilians, including former head of state Olusegun Obasanjo. Journalists Kunle Ajibade, Chris Anyanwu, George Mbah and Ben Charles-Obi had reported on the alleged plot; the government said their reporting exposed security information and cast doubt on the coup allegation. A Special Military Tribunal, a panel of military officers with no requirement to observe ordinary court procedure or allow appeal, tried the journalists alongside the alleged plotters and convicted them as "accessories after the fact to treason." Ajibade received a life sentence, later commuted to 15 years; Anyanwu received 15 years; Mbah and Charles-Obi received 15 years each. One tribunal official said the prosecutions were meant "to deter others from the irresponsibilities of Nigerian journalism." The Committee to Protect Journalists said the case was part of a broader campaign using indefinite detention, secret military trials and violence against Nigeria's independent press.{c:246}{c:247}{c:248}{c:249}
stated_justification: A security official told one journalist the story "had caused some security problems and discredited the government's coup allegation"; a tribunal official said the prosecutions were meant "to deter others from the irresponsibilities of Nigerian journalism."{c:247}{c:248}
effect_on_reporting: Four journalists received prison terms of up to 15 years with no right of appeal for reporting on a coup allegation the government itself had announced, part of what CPJ called "a calculated, and almost successful, campaign to decimate" Nigeria's independent press.{c:246}{c:247}{c:248}{c:249}

title: Malaysia pressures domestic media and monitors foreign correspondents after arresting former deputy premier Anwar Ibrahim
issue_of_the_day: The September 1998 dismissal, arrest and prosecution of former deputy prime minister Anwar Ibrahim on corruption and sodomy charges.
outcome_note: The sources reviewed do not describe a formal reversal of the surveillance of journalists or the pressure on party-linked papers during this period.
summary: After Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's government arrested former deputy prime minister Anwar Ibrahim in September 1998, party-linked newspapers pressured staff to follow the official line, police visited journalists who interviewed his wife, and authorities said they would monitor internet traffic about the case.{c:250}{c:251}{c:252}{c:253}{c:254}
what_happened: On September 20, 1998, Malaysian police arrested former deputy prime minister Anwar Ibrahim, days after Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad dismissed him amid a political dispute; Anwar was later convicted on corruption and sodomy charges he said were fabricated to end his political career. Newspapers partly owned by the ruling United Malays National Organisation (UMNO), including Utusan Malaysia, pressured editors and journalists to follow the party line on the case or face dismissal, Human Rights Watch reported. Police visited foreign correspondents in Singapore who had interviewed Anwar's wife, Wan Azizah, as part of a sedition investigation into her, and authorities barred her from addressing public meetings. The government also announced it would monitor internet traffic discussing the arrest. Circulation of the opposition paper Harakah surged roughly fourfold as readers sought coverage outside the mainstream press; its editor, Zulkifli Sulong, was later charged with sedition and said, "The government is trying to silence us."{c:250}{c:251}{c:252}{c:253}{c:254}
stated_justification: Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said restrictions on coverage of the case were necessary "to preserve national harmony" and pointed to what he called fabrications by foreign news outlets, while saying in a separate speech, "A government which controls the media is a government with no morals."{c:253}
effect_on_reporting: Party-linked newspapers pressured journalists to follow the government's account or risk dismissal, police investigated reporters over interviews with Anwar's wife, and the opposition paper Harakah, whose circulation surged, later saw its editor charged with sedition.{c:252}{c:254}

title: State-controlled Gazprom takes formal control of Russia's independent NTV television network
issue_of_the_day: NTV's critical coverage of Russia's second war in Chechnya and of the government of President Vladimir Putin, who had taken office in May 2000.
outcome_note: The takeover was not reversed; most of NTV's original staff resigned in the following weeks rather than work under the new management.
summary: Gazprom, Russia's state-controlled gas company, used debts owed by NTV's parent company to take control of the country's last major independent television network at a shareholders' meeting, replacing its owner and top editors with its own appointees.{c:255}{c:256}{c:257}{c:258}
what_happened: NTV, founded by media entrepreneur Vladimir Gusinsky, was Russia's most-watched independent television network and had criticized the government's conduct of the war in Chechnya. Gazprom, Russia's state-controlled gas company, had extended loans to Gusinsky's holding company, Media-Most, and after Gusinsky left Russia facing separate criminal proceedings, Gazprom called in the debt and obtained enough shares to control NTV. On April 14, 2001, Gazprom-Media used a shareholders' meeting to take formal control, removing Gusinsky and managing director Yevgeny Kiselyov from the board and installing Alfred Kokh as chairman and Boris Jordan as general director. NTV staff said in a statement, "We realize that the ultimate goal of this meeting ... is establishing full control over our company." Gusinsky and Kiselyov said the takeover was a Kremlin-directed effort to end independent national television under President Vladimir Putin. The Committee to Protect Journalists said it was "very concerned about Gazprom-Media's potential interference in the editorial decisions of NTV journalists."{c:255}{c:256}{c:257}{c:258}
stated_justification: Gazprom framed the takeover as debt collection from Gusinsky's Media-Most holding company; Gusinsky and Kiselyov said it was, in substance, "a Kremlin-directed campaign to rein in Russia's only remaining independent national TV station."{c:257}
effect_on_reporting: NTV's founder and top editorial leadership were removed and replaced with Gazprom appointees; CPJ said it remained "very concerned about Gazprom-Media's potential interference in the editorial decisions of NTV journalists" going forward.{c:258}

title: Zimbabwe enacts a law requiring all journalists and media houses to hold government licenses
issue_of_the_day: Zimbabwe's contested March 2002 presidential election, in which President Mugabe faced international criticism over the vote's conduct.
outcome_note: The record reviewed documents a 2007 amendment easing individual accreditation but does not establish to day precision when AIPPA's licensing framework was repealed.
summary: Zimbabwe's parliament passed the Access to Information and Protection of Privacy Act (AIPPA), requiring every journalist and media company to obtain a government license renewed every two years, weeks before a closely contested 2002 presidential election.{c:259}{c:260}{c:261}{c:262}
what_happened: In March 2002, weeks before a presidential election, Zimbabwe's government, led by President Robert Mugabe, enacted the Access to Information and Protection of Privacy Act (AIPPA). The law required every journalist and media company to be licensed by a government-appointed regulator, the Media and Information Commission, with licenses renewable every two years, and created new offenses for publishing information officials deemed false. Freedom House said the law "requires all journalists and media companies to be licensed, imposes strict content restrictions, and grants broad powers to a government-controlled regulator." Independent outlets and press-freedom groups opposed the law in principle, saying statutory licensing of print media had no place in a democracy; some foreign correspondents were denied accreditation and independent papers, including the Daily News, were later prosecuted for operating without a license. A 2007 amendment eased individual accreditation requirements outside covering Parliament or official events, but Freedom House said the framework remained "extremely restrictive."{c:259}{c:260}{c:261}{c:262}
stated_justification: The law's licensing and content provisions were presented as regulating professional standards and accountability in the media; the sources reviewed did not record a specific quoted government defense beyond the law's own grant of power to a state-appointed regulator.{c:259}{c:260}{c:261}{c:262}
effect_on_reporting: Every journalist and media house needed a government-issued, renewable license to operate; independent outlets that published without one, including the Daily News, faced closure, and Freedom House called the framework "extremely restrictive, with onerous licensing requirements."{c:261}{c:262}

title: Investigative journalist Anna Politkovskaya is shot dead in Moscow; a former police officer is later convicted of organizing the killing
issue_of_the_day: Politkovskaya's investigative reporting on human-rights abuses in Chechnya and her criticism of the Russian government's conduct there.
outcome_note: Courts convicted and sentenced five men, including former police officer Dmitry Pavlyuchenkov, for organizing or carrying out the killing; who ordered it was never conclusively established in court.
summary: Anna Politkovskaya, a Novaya Gazeta journalist known for reporting critical of Russia's conduct of the war in Chechnya, was shot dead in her Moscow apartment building; a Moscow court later convicted a former police officer of organizing surveillance for her killers.{c:263}{c:264}{c:265}{c:266}{c:267}{c:268}
what_happened: Anna Politkovskaya, a reporter for the independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta, was known for reporting on human-rights abuses during Russia's war in Chechnya, a mostly Muslim region in Russia's North Caucasus, and for criticism of President Vladimir Putin's government. On October 7, 2006, Putin's birthday, she was shot dead in the elevator of her Moscow apartment building. Investigators eventually charged several men, including Sergei Khadzhikurbanov, reported as a former police officer, and, later, Dmitry Pavlyuchenkov, a former officer in a Moscow police surveillance unit, who pleaded guilty in 2012 to tracking Politkovskaya's movements and supplying the gun used to kill her. A Moscow court sentenced Pavlyuchenkov to 11 years in exchange for his cooperation; he told the court, "I want to appeal to the family of Anna Stepanovna; I simply want to ask for their human forgiveness." Five men were eventually convicted; who ordered the killing was never conclusively established in court. The Kremlin did not immediately comment on her death.{c:263}{c:264}{c:265}{c:266}{c:267}{c:268}
stated_justification: No government body said it was responsible or offered a public justification; investigators built their case around the men convicted of organizing and carrying out the killing, including a former police surveillance officer, without conclusively naming who ordered it.{c:263}{c:264}{c:265}{c:266}{c:267}{c:268}
effect_on_reporting: The Russian Union of Journalists' Igor Yakovenko called it "clearly a contract killing," and the International Federation of Journalists said it "reflects on the state of lawlessness that is threatening to overwhelm the whole of Russian journalism."{c:264}{c:265}
ladder_note: Who ordered the killing was never conclusively established in court.

title: Iran expels a BBC correspondent and restricts foreign journalists after a disputed 2009 election
issue_of_the_day: Iran's disputed June 12, 2009 presidential election and the mass protests that followed allegations the vote was rigged for incumbent Mahmoud Ahmadinejad.
outcome_note: The sources reviewed do not establish when Iran lifted the specific 2009 restrictions on foreign correspondents covering the post-election protests.
summary: After Iran's disputed June 2009 presidential election produced mass protests, the government expelled BBC correspondent Jon Leyne, revoked foreign press credentials, confined most foreign journalists to office-based reporting, and blocked access to numerous websites.{c:269}{c:270}{c:271}
what_happened: Iran's June 12, 2009 presidential election, which officials declared a large win for incumbent Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, prompted mass street protests over allegations of fraud. The government accused foreign media of inciting unrest; the state Fars news agency accused BBC correspondent Jon Leyne of "dispatching fabricated news and reports, ignoring neutrality in news, supporting rioters and trampling the Iranian nation's rights," and authorities ordered him to leave the country. The government revoked accreditation for many foreign journalists, barred them from reporting from the streets, and permitted only phone interviews and official government sources; Al Arabiya's Tehran operation was temporarily suspended. Foreign minister Manouchehr Mottaki called the election "a very transparent competition" and accused Britain of interference without providing evidence. Some journalists, including The New York Times' Roger Cohen, continued reporting despite the restrictions. Authorities also blocked numerous websites and limited mobile-phone text messaging during the unrest that followed.{c:269}{c:270}{c:271}
stated_justification: State media accused BBC correspondent Jon Leyne of "dispatching fabricated news and reports, ignoring neutrality in news, supporting rioters and trampling the Iranian nation's rights"; Foreign Minister Manouchehr Mottaki called the election "a very transparent competition" and blamed unrest on foreign interference.{c:269}{c:270}
effect_on_reporting: Foreign correspondents lost accreditation and were confined largely to phone interviews and official sources rather than street reporting; one report said the government revoked all foreign press passes during the unrest, forcing some journalists to work without official credentials.{c:271}

title: Hungary's parliament gives a government-appointed media council power to fine outlets for unbalanced coverage
issue_of_the_day: The incoming Fidesz government's broader effort, after its April 2010 election win, to restructure Hungary's state institutions, including media regulation.
outcome_note: The law took effect January 1, 2011, and, after European Union criticism, Hungary amended some provisions in 2011 but kept the media authority's core licensing and fining powers.
summary: Hungary's parliament, controlled by Prime Minister Viktor Orban's Fidesz party, passed a media law creating a government-appointed National Media and Infocommunications Authority empowered to fine any outlet, print, broadcast or online, for coverage it deemed unbalanced or offensive to public morality.{c:272}{c:273}{c:274}{c:275}
what_happened: In December 2010, Hungary's parliament, where Prime Minister Viktor Orban's Fidesz party held a two-thirds majority, passed a media law creating the National Media and Infocommunications Authority, a regulator whose board is appointed by the parliamentary majority for nine-year terms. The law let the authority impose fines, reported at up to roughly half a million dollars per violation, on any news outlet it judged had produced "unbalanced" coverage or violated vaguely defined standards of "public morality," and required outlets to register with the state. The law took effect January 1, 2011. The Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe called the media council's power "unprecedented in European democracies," and former European Union Commissioner Laszlo Kovacs said, "The law provides total control to the government over all the media, both public and private." Orban said the government was "monitoring its practical application" and would address concerns if verified; a Media Council legal official acknowledged the country's earlier "unfettered press freedom" had also produced problems.{c:272}{c:273}{c:274}{c:275}
stated_justification: Prime Minister Orban said the government was "monitoring its practical application and if any of the political concerns are verified ... we are ready to remedy them," while a Media Council legal official said Hungary's earlier "unfettered press freedom" had "yielded some negative fruit as well."{c:273}{c:274}
effect_on_reporting: Every news outlet, print, broadcast or online, became subject to fines of up to roughly half a million dollars for coverage a government-appointed board deemed unbalanced; the OSCE called the board's power "unprecedented in European democracies."{c:275}

title: Ecuador's Organic Communication Law creates a regulator that issues hundreds of sanctions against journalists and outlets
issue_of_the_day: President Correa's long-running public disputes with Ecuadorian media over their coverage of his government, including a separate 2011 libel case against the newspaper El Universo.
outcome_note: President Lenin Moreno's government moved to eliminate SUPERCOM in 2018, and the reform of the Communication Law was published in the Official Register on February 20, 2019; Fundamedios director Cesar Ricaurte said the surrounding legal framework nonetheless remained "intact."
summary: Ecuador's National Assembly passed the Organic Communication Law under President Rafael Correa, creating the Superintendency of Information and Communication (SUPERCOM), a regulator that issued more than 675 sanctions against journalists and media outlets over the following four years.{c:276}{c:277}{c:278}{c:279}
what_happened: On June 25, 2013, Ecuador's National Assembly, controlled by allies of President Rafael Correa, passed the Organic Communication Law, which created the Superintendency of Information and Communication (SUPERCOM), a regulator empowered to fine, reprimand or order public apologies from journalists and outlets found to have violated the law's content rules, provisions the United Nations and the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights said were used against coverage unfavorable to the government. Within four years, SUPERCOM had opened 1,081 cases and issued 675 sanctions, by its own count, split by the monitoring group Fundamedios into 324 fines, 137 written reprimands and 54 forced public apologies. SUPERCOM itself said the law guaranteed rather than restricted press freedom because "in four years no media outlet has been closed." After Correa left office, President Lenin Moreno proposed eliminating SUPERCOM in 2018; his communications secretary said, "If we're in a constructive process, we should get rid of the Supercom."{c:276}{c:277}{c:278}{c:279}
stated_justification: SUPERCOM described its own record as evidence the law protected rather than restricted the press, saying "in four years no media outlet has been closed," while United Nations and Inter-American human-rights bodies said the law had been "used as an instrument to unduly interfere in the content of media outlets and punish them, especially when their coverage is unfavorable."{c:278}
effect_on_reporting: SUPERCOM opened 1,081 cases and issued 675 sanctions against journalists and outlets in four years, including fines, written reprimands and forced public apologies, a pattern Fundamedios and international monitors said pressured critical coverage.{c:276}{c:277}{c:278}{c:279}

title: Egypt arrests and later convicts three Al Jazeera journalists on terrorism-related charges
issue_of_the_day: The Egyptian military's July 2013 removal of President Mohamed Morsi and the government's subsequent designation of his Muslim Brotherhood as a terrorist organization.
outcome_note: President Sisi pardoned Fahmy and Mohamed on September 23, 2015; Greste had already been deported to Australia in February 2015 under a prisoner-transfer arrangement.
summary: Months after the military removed President Mohamed Morsi, Egyptian security forces arrested Al Jazeera English journalists Peter Greste, Mohamed Fahmy and Baher Mohamed at a Cairo hotel; courts later convicted them of aiding a banned organization, and international pressure led to pardons.{c:280}{c:281}{c:282}{c:283}{c:284}
what_happened: On December 29, 2013, Egyptian security forces arrested Al Jazeera English correspondent Peter Greste, bureau chief Mohamed Fahmy and producer Baher Mohamed at Cairo's Marriott Hotel, months after the military, led by then-Defense Minister Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, removed elected President Mohamed Morsi of the Muslim Brotherhood, which the government later designated a terrorist organization. Prosecutors charged the journalists with aiding the Brotherhood and "spreading false news"; a June 2014 trial convicted them, and an August 2015 retrial, after the first conviction was overturned on appeal, again found them guilty of "aiding a terrorist organisation," partly, the judge said, because they had not registered with the country's journalist "syndicate," sentencing Fahmy and Mohamed to three years. Al Jazeera called the verdict "a deliberate attack on press freedom"; Greste, already deported and tried in absentia, said, "We did nothing wrong. The court presented no evidence." President Sisi pardoned Fahmy and Mohamed on September 23, 2015, as part of a wider amnesty.{c:280}{c:281}{c:282}{c:283}{c:284}
stated_justification: Prosecutors charged the journalists with aiding the banned Muslim Brotherhood and "spreading false news"; the August 2015 judge cited, in part, their failure to register with the country's official journalist "syndicate" and unauthorized broadcast equipment.{c:281}
effect_on_reporting: All three lost their liberty for over a year on charges press-freedom groups said lacked evidence; Al Jazeera said the verdict was "yet another deliberate attack on press freedom," and the United Nations said it was "very disturbed" by the sentences.{c:282}{c:283}

title: Poland's new government gains power to replace public broadcaster leadership, and journalists are dismissed
issue_of_the_day: Law and Justice's decisive October 2015 election win and its stated aim of overhauling public institutions it viewed as insufficiently accountable to voters.
outcome_note: The appointment power and pattern of dismissals continued through the remainder of the PiS government's term; ownership of the public broadcasters changed only after a later change of government.
summary: Weeks after winning power, Poland's Law and Justice (PiS) party passed a law letting the treasury minister directly appoint and dismiss the heads of public radio and television, and dozens of journalists at the public broadcaster were subsequently dismissed or resigned.{c:285}{c:286}{c:287}{c:288}
what_happened: Poland's Law and Justice (PiS) party won parliamentary and presidential elections in 2015 and, within weeks of taking office, passed a "small" media law, signed by President Andrzej Duda on December 31, 2015, giving the treasury minister power to appoint and dismiss the heads of public radio and television broadcasters directly, without the previously required independent broadcasting council process. Reporters Without Borders said the law "gave the ruling party close control of the public media." Under Prime Minister Beata Szydlo's government, dozens of journalists and executives at the public broadcasters TVP and Polish Radio were dismissed or resigned in the following months, part of what one former colleague called a "political cleansing" that began at the top and moved through the ranks, affecting first "journalists and editors of news and current affairs programmes." RSF said firing "experienced journalists whose professionalism has never been disputed violates a democratic society's rules and threatens press freedom," and that the changes "helped precipitate Poland's rapid fall" in its press-freedom rankings.{c:285}{c:286}{c:287}{c:288}
stated_justification: The government did not offer an individualized public justification for each dismissal in the sources reviewed; a former colleague of those removed described management as seeking staff viewed as ideologically reliable rather than only professionally qualified.{c:285}{c:286}{c:287}{c:288}
effect_on_reporting: RSF said the dismissals of experienced, professionally undisputed journalists violated "a democratic society's rules and threatens press freedom" and "badly hurt the quality of public radio programmes," contributing to Poland's fall in press-freedom rankings.{c:286}{c:287}

title: Cambodia's government forces the closure of The Cambodia Daily with a disputed multimillion-dollar tax bill
issue_of_the_day: Preparations for Cambodia's 2018 general election and a wider government campaign against independent media and civil-society groups seen as sympathetic to the opposition.
outcome_note: The Cambodia Daily did not reopen; its closure coincided with a wider campaign against independent outlets and civil-society groups ahead of Cambodia's 2018 election.
