title: Russia: new laws penalize online "fake news" and "disrespecting authorities"
issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
outcome_note: The laws were enacted and were later expanded in March 2022 to include prison terms of up to 15 years for wartime 'fakes.'
summary: Russia's parliament passed laws letting courts jail and fine people, including journalists, for posting information the government alone judges to be false, or for statements found to disrespect officials or state symbols online.{c:684}{c:685}{c:686}
what_happened:
On March 7, 2019, Russia's State Duma passed legislation permitting courts to jail and fine people who use the internet to spread what the law calls "fake news" or to disrespect government officials and state symbols, including President Vladimir Putin. Under the fake-news provisions, individuals, including journalists, could be fined up to 100,000 rubles, and companies up to 500,000 rubles, for posting unverified information that authorities determine threatens someone's life, health or property, or threatens mass public disorder. Separately, people found guilty of posting what courts call indecent statements about the government could face up to 15 days in administrative detention, with fines rising to 200,000 rubles and repeat violations carrying additional jail time. CPJ said the legislation was clearly aimed at tightening state control over independent media and pressuring journalists into restraining their own reporting.{c:684}{c:685}{c:686}

Sustained; the laws remained in force and were later expanded during the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.{c:684}{c:685}{c:686}
stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed.{c:684}{c:685}{c:686}
effect_on_reporting: The law gave authorities a standing legal tool to fine or briefly jail journalists and ordinary internet users over reporting or commentary the government alone determined to be false or disrespectful, without a specific factual dispute needing to be argued in court beforehand.{c:686}
unknowns: The sources reviewed do not report how many people were fined or jailed under the law in its first year.
ladder_note: Russia's parliament created fines and jail terms for online posts that authorities alone judge false or disrespectful of officials; no enacted United States law imposes jail time for calling an official statement false.

title: Russia: independent outlet Meduza designated a 'foreign agent'
issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
outcome_note: The designation was not reversed; Russia later declared Meduza an 'undesirable organization' and outlawed it entirely.
summary: Russia's Justice Ministry labeled the independent news site Meduza and outlet PASMI "foreign agents," a status requiring constant public disclosure, quarterly reports and audits, and carrying up to two years in prison for noncompliance, which Meduza said would destroy its advertising business.{c:687}{c:688}{c:689}
what_happened:
On April 23, 2021, Russia's Justice Ministry added the independent news site Meduza, which is based in Latvia and widely read inside Russia, and the outlet PASMI to its register of "foreign agents." The designation, created under a law expanded over several years to cover media organizations and individuals, requires labeled outlets to mark every piece of content with a foreign agent notice, provide a legal representative inside Russia, file quarterly financial reports and semi-annual activity reports, and undergo annual audits. People working for a foreign agent outlet who fail to comply can face up to two years in prison. Meduza's editor said the label would deprive the outlet of the ability to fully practice journalism inside Russia and would destroy its business, since advertisers would avoid being associated with a designated outlet. CPJ called on Russia to stop labeling independent outlets as foreign agents.{c:687}{c:688}{c:689}

Sustained; the designation remained in place and Russia later outlawed Meduza entirely.{c:687}{c:688}{c:689}
stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed.{c:687}{c:688}{c:689}
effect_on_reporting: Meduza's editor said the label would cut off the outlet's advertising revenue and constrain its ability to operate as a normal news organization inside Russia, years before Russia banned it outright in 2023.{c:689}
unknowns: The sources reviewed do not give the Justice Ministry's specific stated reason for designating Meduza on that date.
ladder_note: Russia's foreign agent label forced an outlet to mark every article, file quarterly reports and risk two years in prison for lapses, by its own editor's account destroying its advertising business; no United States "fake news" designation carries a legal reporting duty or prison exposure.

title: Egypt: media law used to fine and block news site al-Mashhad
issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
outcome_note: Al-Mashhad's website was still inaccessible in Egypt as of May 7, 2019, the last date given in the source reviewed.
summary: Under a 2018 law that treats any social media account with more than 5,000 followers as a media outlet, Egypt's media regulator fined news site al-Mashhad and ordered internet providers to block it for spreading what it called false news.{c:690}{c:691}{c:692}
what_happened:
Egypt's Law No. 180 of 2018 applies to every online and offline media outlet and, separately, to any social media account with more than 5,000 followers, treating such accounts as media outlets subject to regulation by the state's Supreme Council for Media Regulation. The law bans content the council judges to be false news, defamatory, obscene, or a threat to national security, with violators facing fines of up to 250,000 Egyptian pounds and having their websites blocked. On March 22, 2019, the council fined the news site al-Mashhad 50,000 Egyptian pounds and ordered Egyptian internet providers to block the site for six months. Al-Mashhad appealed, and on April 7 the council reduced the block to one month starting from the appeal date, but the site remained inaccessible inside Egypt as of May 7, 2019, according to the source reviewed.{c:690}{c:691}{c:692}

Unresolved; al-Mashhad remained blocked in Egypt as of the date given in the source reviewed.{c:690}{c:691}{c:692}
stated_justification: Not stated in the sources reviewed.{c:690}{c:691}{c:692}
effect_on_reporting: The law let a state regulator fine and block a news site inside the country over content it alone judged false, without the matter going before an ordinary court first.{c:692}
unknowns: The sources reviewed do not report whether the block was lifted after May 7, 2019.
ladder_note: Egyptian law classifies any social media account over five thousand followers as a media outlet subject to state fines and blocking, and Egypt used it to fine and block a news site for weeks; no United States "fake news" designation can fine or block an outlet.

title: Belarus: Deutsche Welle and other outlets labeled 'extremist'
issue_of_the_day: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
outcome_note: The designation brought the total number of outlets labeled extremist in Belarus to 20 and was not reported as reversed.
summary: A Minsk court declared all output from German broadcaster Deutsche Welle "extremist," alongside a local newspaper and a Russian blogger's videos, making it a crime to produce, store or share the labeled material, as a former correspondent was jailed the same week.{c:695}{c:696}{c:697}{c:698}
what_happened:
